title: T1021.003 — Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Remote Services: Distributed Component Object Model with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: Animated attack simulation: DCOM lateral movement

steps.title: Why DCOM? No files needed
steps.caption: DCOM lets a program on one computer use a building block (a COM object) inside a program on another computer. Attackers use it to run commands remotely with only built-in Windows features. This attacker already holds the svc_admin password, and svc_admin is a local admin on WS-B.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

fields.detail: DCOM lets a program on one computer use a building block (a COM object) inside a program on another

detection.detail: This activity is not visible to the victim yet.

steps.title: Check the RPC door (port 135)
steps.caption: Before touching DCOM, the attacker checks the RPC endpoint mapper on TCP port 135. If this door answers, a remote COM activation is possible. A Sysmon 3 record on WS-A shows the check going out.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Ask WS-B for a COM object
steps.caption: The attacker asks Windows on WS-B to create the MMC20.Application object remotely. WS-B logs a Type 3 network logon, and the real DCOM session continues on a dynamic RPC port. No file is transferred.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Run a command inside MMC on WS-B
steps.caption: The attacker presses the ExecuteShellCommand button on the remote object. On WS-B, mmc.exe becomes the parent of cmd.exe - a GUI admin tool spawning a shell, which is the key artifact of this technique. The command writes its output to the C$ admin share.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Grab the output over the admin share
steps.caption: The attacker reads the result back with a normal admin-share path. To WS-B this looks like a file-share read by svc_admin, logged as a 5145 event. A small step - but it ties the SMB traffic to the same pair of hosts.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Another object: ShellBrowserWindow on APP01
steps.caption: The attacker repeats the trick on the app server with a different object: ShellBrowserWindow.Application. Its ShellExecute method starts encoded PowerShell on APP01. The tell: the parent is explorer.exe, on a server where nobody is logged in.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: Dump credentials on APP01
steps.caption: With code running on APP01, the attacker reads the memory of lsass.exe using rundll32 and comsvcs.dll. The dump holds more credentials, which would let the attack reach even more machines. ProcessAccess and process-creation events catch both moments.
steps.defender: Edge, DNS and network-flow telemetry provide the first reliable evidence.

steps.title: How defenders catch this attack
steps.caption: The SOC searches for the impossible pair: mmc.exe or explorer.exe spawning shells where no user sits. One query pulls the whole story together, and the four chips below match the rules in section 4 of this guide.
